The knowledge base doesn't use the term "incident commander," so I can't confirm that title exists at Halcyon. The closest equivalent is the charge nurse, who coordinates the immediate response to a patient safety event.

- **Charge nurse (main coordinator):** The charge nurse on shift coordinates the immediate response. That includes assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records [2]. In a large clinic, the charge nurse coordinates the response to any patient safety event [1].
- **Clinic manager (fallback):** If there is no charge nurse on shift, the event is reported to the clinic manager instead [2]. In medium and small clinics, a charge nurse is designated only when two or more RNs are on shift; otherwise the clinic manager fills that role [1]. The clinic manager is also the escalation point for a site with no charge nurse on shift [3]. So the clinic manager is the person coordinating at a clinic without a charge nurse.
- **On-call medical director (escalation, not coordination):** For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [2]. The on-call medical director is reached through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [4].

The older 2025 staffing standard says a charge nurse is designated whenever two or more RNs are on shift. It doesn't mention the clinic manager fallback, so it appears to be superseded by the September 2026 version [6][1].

Halcyon's documents require a signed business associate agreement (BAA), a security risk assessment, and a systems inventory entry before a vendor handles PHI. They do not use the term "DPA," and they don't spell out a full vendor approval sign-off chain.

**What's required**

- **Signed BAA, before any PHI is disclosed.** A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI for Halcyon is a business associate. No PHI may be shared until the BAA is executed, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [1].
- **Security risk assessment.** New systems that will hold PHI need one [6]. For AI tools, the list is a security risk assessment, a signed BAA, an inventory entry, and for clinical use a CMIO clinical safety review [2]. The CSCAB chair reminded the board on October 28, 2026 that a new place where PHI is stored needs a security risk assessment and an inventory entry before go-live, not after [8].
- **Systems inventory entry.** The inventory is the list of systems approved to hold PHI, and new PHI systems need an entry before go-live. Email the HIPAA Security Officer [6]. The sources say "before go-live" rather than "before any data is shared," so confirm with the Security Officer whether the entry must come before the first test file.

**Approval steps**

For tools that will handle PHI, email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) [2]. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2]. The sources don't describe a formal sign-off form or a separate step for general vendors.

**DPA**

The knowledge base doesn't mention a data processing agreement or DPA. The only contract requirement it defines is the BAA. If your team uses a DPA as well, the sources don't say whether it is required or how it relates to the BAA, so check with the Privacy Officer.

**Example:** Tallgrass Survey Co. has a completed security risk assessment (passed with conditions, September 2026) but no executed BAA. Halcyon is still negotiating retention, with Tallgrass asking for 5 years and Halcyon offering 18 months. No PHI can go to Tallgrass until the BAA is signed [1].

Northwind has a break-glass-style process, but it covers a different situation. It is for engineers reaching **customer workspaces** during support cases, not for clinicians opening patient charts. The knowledge base doesn't describe an internal-systems equivalent or anything like Halcyon's chart restrictions.

**How Northwind's process works**
- **Trigger:** An open support case or declared incident only. "Curiosity" and "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [7].
- **Approval:** A second engineer from support or on-call must approve in Teleport. The approver can't be the requester or on the same case [7].
- **Duration:** 2 hours, shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [7][8].
- **Access level:** Read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case [7].
- **Recording and review:** Sessions are recorded for one year. The customer's audit log shows the access, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security reviews a weekly sample of sessions, plus every session that used write access [7].

**How it differs from Halcyon's Meridian break-the-glass**

| | Halcyon (Meridian EHR) | Northwind (customer workspaces) |
|---|---|---|
| Approval | None in the moment; manager confirms the reason afterward if unclear [1] | Second engineer must approve before access [7] |
| Duration | Until end of shift, up to 12 hours [1] | 2 hours [7] |
| Review | Every event reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days [1] | Weekly sample plus all write-access sessions [7] |
| Misuse | Inappropriate use is a privacy incident and may lead to sanctions up to termination [1] | Personal-relationship access is prohibited [7] |
| Customer notice | Not described | Admins emailed within 24 hours [7] |

**Gaps in the knowledge base**
- No internal-systems or chart-style restriction equivalent for Northwind staff was found.
- No reviewer turnaround time is documented for Northwind's weekly sample.
- No manager-confirmation step is documented for Northwind.
- No sanctions policy specific to emergency-access misuse was found. The only stated prohibition is looking at a workspace belonging to someone the engineer knows personally [7]. The general security policy covers access control but says nothing about discipline [8].

**Short answer: No for patient data at Halcyon, and no for restricted customer data at Northwind. For other sensitive data, the knowledge base doesn't say whether Slack is allowed.**

**Northwind Labs**
- Restricted data, such as customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys, never leaves production and is never allowed in tickets or Slack [1]. The emergency-access rules repeat this: don't paste payloads into Slack, and use field names and counts instead [3].
- Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared "on a need-to-know basis" [1]. That is the only handling rule given for these classes. The sources don't say whether Slack is allowed for them.
- Personal devices may be used for Slack and email through the managed mobile apps [1]. This doesn't address what content may go in Slack.
- If you see sensitive data you didn't expect, report it in `#security-help` [1][3].

**Halcyon Health**
- Slack is listed as "Never, including DMs" for PHI [2].
- Email is the approved route for PHI, using `[secure]` encrypted email with PHI kept out of the subject line [2].
- Halcyon's AI tool rules also say patient details must be treated as PHI even after names are removed [4].

**What's missing**
- Northwind: no source says whether confidential or other non-customer sensitive data (employee data, financials, contracts) may appear in Slack, or whether it is restricted there. The only guidance is need-to-know.
- Halcyon: no source covers non-PHI sensitive data in Slack, such as staff HR matters or internal financials, or says whether any exception exists. The Slack ban is stated only for PHI.

For either company, check with the Security team at Northwind (`#security-help`) or the Privacy Officer at Halcyon (privacy@halcyon.example) before posting anything sensitive that isn't covered above.

You need sign-off from the Platform team's change approver, plus the Head of Security because Driftwood holds Restricted data.

- **Platform change approver:** Oluwaseun Adeyemi (Seun). His delegate is Kofi Mensah. [5]
- **Head of Security:** Tomasz Wierzbicki, or the security on-call delegate. [5]

**Why these approvers:**
- Driftwood is the long-term event archive, and the service catalog lists its owner as PLAT [6].
- Driftwood is classified as Restricted [6]. Its archived event payloads are customer event payloads [6], and the information security policy classifies customer event payloads as Restricted [7]. So the security sign-off applies.
- Lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets are a normal change under the production change approval policy [2]. Normal changes to a Restricted service also need security sign-off [1].

**Other requirements:**
- Retention changes need an ADR, and the ADR must be linked from the PR [1].
- Shortening retention needs a 30-day customer notice from the account team for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period [1].
- Add the `change:normal` label to the PR, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. For Restricted services, also request `@northwind/security` [1].
- Approvals expire after 7 days, so re-request if the change hasn't shipped by then [1].
- The holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, when only standard and emergency changes are allowed [1].

**What the sources don't cover:** I found no source stating whether a particular lifecycle rule change is treated differently from other retention changes by the security team. Confirm with Tomasz Wierzbicki or the security on-call if the change is unusual. Also, the retention standard says Enterprise customers can contract for up to 730 days of archive retention with security approval, but that doesn't change who signs off on the rule itself [2].

A Growth customer can send the bulk endpoint, `POST /v2/events/batch`, at **50 requests per second**, with up to **10,000 events or 10 MB per request**. Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Short bursts up to 2x (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds. Over the limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [2].

**Plan match:** The $1,200-a-month plan is Growth [1]. Growth is the column used in the rate limit table [2].

**Raising the limit:**
- Growth limits are fixed by contract. Apart from one-off backfill raises, customers who need more are pointed to sales about Enterprise [2].
- Enterprise ingest limits can be raised up to 3x the default by contract, through a request in the DP queue [2]. The sources don't say outright that Growth is ineligible for this, but the wording implies it.
- A temporary raise for a one-off backfill can be granted by the DP on-call primary, for up to 72 hours, on any plan that has the endpoint [2]. The sources give no multiplier or resulting rate for Growth, so I can't tell you the raised number.

**A year of history:** The sources don't say how long a year-long backfill would take at these rates, or how to handle one that won't fit a 72-hour raise window. They also don't give the customer's historical event volume. The customer should estimate their event count and divide by the rate (50 req/s × 10,000 events = up to 500,000 events/s, before any raise). Then they should ask DP whether the job fits the window or needs a plan.

labels.text: A Growth customer can send the bulk endpoint, POST /v2/events/batch, at 50 requests per second, with up to 10,000 events or 10 MB per request.
Limits are per workspace, not per API key.
Short bursts up to 2x (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds.
Over the limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
Plan match: The $1,200-a-month plan is Growth.
Growth is the column used in the rate limit table.
Raising the limit
Growth limits are fixed by contract.
Apart from one-off backfill raises, customers who need more are pointed to sales about Enterprise.
Enterprise ingest limits can be raised up to 3x the default by contract, through a request in the DP queue.
The sources don't say outright that Growth is ineligible for this, but the wording implies it.
A temporary raise for a one-off backfill can be granted by the DP on-call primary, for up to 72 hours, on any plan that has the endpoint.
The sources give no multiplier or resulting rate for Growth, so I can't tell you the raised number.
A year of history: The sources don't say how long a year-long backfill would take at these rates, or how to handle one that won't fit a 72-hour raise window.
They also don't give the customer's historical event volume.
The customer should estimate their event count and divide by the rate (50 req/s × 10,000 events = up to 500,000 events/s, before any raise).
Then they should ask DP whether the job fits the window or needs a plan.

On Wednesday, November 18, the November 2026 rota applies, and the on-call medical director is the senior physician for the whole network [3]. The rota document lists only the Thanksgiving swap and doesn't name the physician for November 18, so use the answering service to reach whoever is on duty.

Riverbend should be scheduling **1.5 medical assistants per physician or nurse practitioner** under the current standard, which took effect September 1, 2026 [1]. The sources don't explicitly record Riverbend's band, though, so that part is inferred.

**Why Medium applies:** Riverbend averaged 46 visits a day in Q3 2026 [3]. The 2026 standard puts 40 to 80 visits a day in the Medium band [1]. The directory says each clinic's band is set from that column every quarter [3]. No source states Riverbend's assigned band directly, so confirm it with Clinical Operations or the clinic manager, Colm Gallagher [3].

**What this means for scheduling:** The Medium band requires at least 2 physicians or NPs on site, and the MA ratio is 1.5 per clinician, rounded up to the next whole person [1]. In practice:
- 2 clinicians on site → 3 MAs (2 × 1.5 = 3)
- 3 clinicians on site → 5 MAs (3 × 1.5 = 4.5, rounded up)

The superseded 2025 standard set Medium clinics at 1.25 MAs per clinician, so don't use that figure [2].

A stopped Bayline results feed is a P1 problem. Bayline must give a first response within **30 minutes**, and the Halcyon person paged is the Integration Services system steward, **Owen Mbeki**.

**Response time.** The vendor matrix defines P1 as any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, with "results not arriving" as its example [2]. Bayline's P1 first response is 30 minutes, and its support runs 24/7 through the interface desk [2]. The matrix describes this as a contractual first response from a qualified engineer, not a resolution time [2].

**Who gets paged.** Clinic staff should open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (ext. 4357 or the intranet tile), not call Bayline directly [2]. For any P1, the Service Desk contacts the vendor and also pages the owning team's system steward [2]. Switchyard, the interface engine that receives Bayline's HL7 feed, is owned by INT and is built in-house with no outside vendor [2][7]. The INT steward is Owen Mbeki (Integration Services) [6].

**Not paged.** The on-call medical director is not the contact for a feed outage. That rota covers clinical escalations, critical results and sentinel events [5]. If the feed stop has already created a patient-safety event, the separate sentinel and adverse event process still applies, so the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [4].

**What the sources don't say.** They don't name a specific on-call engineer for the interface team, and they don't give a named after-hours contact beyond the Service Desk and the steward. The matrix also doesn't name "feed stopped" as a P1 example in those exact words. I inferred that from the "results not arriving" example.

- The catalog does not use the term PHI. It uses Northwind's own data classes [1]. I found no Northwind document that flags systems holding health information, so I can't say whether Northwind handles PHI at all.
- The catalog covers production services. Shared infrastructure, such as Kafka, Kubernetes, managed Postgres and Teleport, appears in a separate table with its own owners: PLAT for most of it and SEC for Teleport [1].

Patient safety events at Halcyon are logged in **SafeReport**, the patient safety reporting system [1][10]. The knowledge base does not state a filing deadline for an ordinary (non-sentinel) event, so I can't give you one.

**Where it gets logged:** SafeReport. Halcyon classifies events on a four-level scale: Level 1 sentinel event, Level 2 adverse event with harm, Level 3 no-harm event, and Level 4 near miss. When unsure, staff report at the higher level, and QPS reclassifies if needed [1].

**Who files:** Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report in SafeReport. Reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**How soon:**
- **Sentinel events:** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1][3]. The on-call director is reached through the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [3].
- **Ordinary events:** The sentinel policy has a "Within 24 hours" section heading, but its body text doesn't give a deadline for filing a SafeReport. I couldn't confirm a 24-hour rule for patient safety events [1].
- **Privacy incidents** are a separate track. Report them to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [4].

**Immediate steps:** Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed. Then tell the charge nurse on shift, or the clinic manager if there is no charge nurse. The charge nurse coordinates the response [1]. The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family [1].

**After filing:** Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis. QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1]. Completed RCAs go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe [1].

**Gaps:** The knowledge base doesn't say how a non-sentinel event is assigned to a level beyond the definitions, or give a deadline for non-sentinel SafeReports. Check with Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) for those.

Northwind's sources don't describe a just-culture framework by that name. They do say postmortems are blameless: "we look at the system and the process, not at individuals. Names appear only in the timeline" [1]. The on-call runbook uses the same "blameless postmortem" wording [3]. Whether Northwind's approach matches your just-culture model in other respects isn't documented, so I can't confirm that.

On authorship, the incident roles FAQ says the IC picks the author, "usually the responder who knew the most about the failure" [1]. The examples in the knowledge base are consistent with that:

- INC-2340 (duplicate invoices): the IC, Kofi Mensah, named Arjun Mehta as postmortem owner when resolving the incident [9].
- INC-2291 (ingest outage): Priya Raman is listed as author, "with the ingest team" [6]. The sources don't say who chose her or whether she was the IC. The incident log lists Oluwaseun Adeyemi as IC [2].

The knowledge base doesn't show a rule that the author is always the IC or always the person who knew most. "Usually" suggests the FAQ allows exceptions, but no source documents them.

Other process details: postmortems are due within five business days of resolution for SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents, and they are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [1][3]. INC-2351 is still in review, with its draft due at the November 5 meeting [2].

Northwind does have a periodic access check, but it doesn't cover EHR access, and the knowledge base doesn't describe a need-to-know check for EHR access at either organization.

**Northwind Labs:** Its information security policy says quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead, and access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [1]. If nobody signs off, the access is removed by default. The same policy covers production access through Teleport, which expires after 8 hours, and revokes all access within one hour of an employee's last working time [1]. The policy doesn't mention EHR systems, and Northwind's materials don't describe an EHR of its own, so this review doesn't apply to EHR access logs.

**Halcyon Health:** Its HIPAA privacy policy says the compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection, and unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [6]. That process looks for anomalous access. The sources don't say whether it also checks whether each user still needs their access, and I found no recertification process or deadline that happens if nobody signs off. The closest related control is that clinical system access is suspended automatically when HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [6].

**What's missing from the knowledge base:**
- Any Northwind review of EHR access, or any Northwind EHR access log review.
- A periodic need-to-know recertification for EHR access at Halcyon, with its frequency or its consequences.
- A documented outcome for unsigned or incomplete Halcyon EHR access reviews.

For the Halcyon question, the Privacy Officer or HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui, per the systems inventory [10]) would be the people to confirm whether a need-to-know recertification exists outside these documents.

Northwind's documents don't say how long the `#vendor-review` process takes or list its steps. The only Northwind rule I found is that any tool that will process customer data must clear that review first [2]. The Halcyon requirements and timeline below come from Halcyon's own policy, which applies to Halcyon staff, not Northwind.

**Halcyon: what it needs before staff use an AI tool with PHI**

Halcyon's policy says PHI can only go into AI tools on its approved list [1][3]. For a new tool that will handle PHI, staff email the Privacy Officer and the HIPAA Security Officer, and the tool needs:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement (BAA) with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [1].

Halcyon says the typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [1].

**Northwind: what I could confirm**

- Any software that will process customer data goes through `#vendor-review` before purchase, regardless of cost [2].
- Northwind's vendor register entries show the kinds of conditions that come out of that review, including signed data processing agreements, SOC 2 reports, and data residency. One vendor is running under a security exception with its DPA still unsigned, and its review passed only on the condition that AI reply suggestions stay disabled until the DPA is signed [4]. I can't confirm from these documents that these are formal requirements for every new tool.

To find Northwind's review timeline, ask the security team or check the `#vendor-review` channel for its intake process.

Halcyon's equivalent is the system steward for the owning team. For the Halcyon app, that is Felix Brandt, but his approval alone is enough only if the change is classed as minor, and the sources don't settle that for bill-pay.

**Who signs off:** The Halcyon app is in the systems inventory under the DHE-PE team (Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement), and the app's functions include bill pay [7]. DHE-PE's system steward is Felix Brandt [1].

**Is his OK enough?** Halcyon's policy splits changes into two classes:
- **Minor changes**, which explicitly include cosmetic changes, need steward approval only [1].
- **Significant changes** affect patient-facing automation, medication information, orders or results routing, clinical decision support, or scheduler/job-runner cutovers. They need three things: the steward's approval, clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao) or her delegate (Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at the weekly CSCAB meeting [1].

Significant changes include "the patient app's clinical content" [1]. The sources don't define that term or say whether the bill-pay screen counts as clinical content. A purely cosmetic change to a payment screen would likely be minor, but that is an inference, not something the policy states.

**What to do:** Confirm the classification with Felix Brandt before you rely on his sign-off alone. If he or the CMIO's office considers the screen clinical content, the change needs CMIO clinical safety sign-off and CSCAB review. The sources don't say how minor changes are recorded, so ask whether a CHG number is required.
